name: Bluish Black
lede: Bluish Black is one of the named blacks in Werner's nomenclature of colors, the system naturalists used to describe slugs, berries and ores before photography.

sections.title: A black in Werner's list
sections.body:
In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner devised a nomenclature of 54 colors to help identify minerals, and revised it over the next forty years or so [1]. The Scottish artist Patrick Syme expanded it to 108 terms in 1814 and to 110 in 1821, adding a painted swatch for each and example species from the animal, vegetable and mineral worlds [1]. Darwin probably met the system as a student in Edinburgh and may have used it on the *Beagle*, although Baty hedges the point [1].

Bluish Black sits among the whites, greys and blacks, numbered 18 in Syme's 1821 edition [2][3]. Syme's recipe for it is velvet black with a little blue and some blackish grey [2]. His examples are the largest black slug, the crowberry and a black cobalt ochre [3]. Neighbors in the lists include greenish black and greyish black; the early lists reproduced by Baty do not agree on the rest of the row, some including iron black or pitch black [2]. Earlier still, in 1769, Schäffer's scheme of seven principal colors already used modifiers such as bluish black and greenish yellow [2].

sections.title: Which bluish black
sections.body:
The swatch here, #413F44, is a scan of an aged Werner swatch, and it leans purple rather than blue [3]. ISCC-NBS 1955 files the nearest block as a dark purplish gray [3]. Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* shows a different Bluish Black on plate XLIX, a much greener, bluer dark, near #31474C [3]. The modifier *bluish* meant different things to different systems.

A related old word shows the same drift. Paterson gives *livid* as bluish, black and blue, lead-colored or pale, a term whose meanings have shifted over time [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 995 works, 4.2 per cent [5]. It is mostly a shadow color, playing that role in 71 per cent of the paintings that carry it [5]. The two largest are Mierevelt's *Portrait of an Elderly Man* of 1630, at 78 per cent of the canvas, and Dou's portrait of his mother, of 1628, at 73 per cent [5].

The lift is strongest in the 1940s, at 5 of 28 works, 4.3 times the archive rate, and among Norwegian paintings, 20 of 120 [5]. [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]] has it in 13 of his 50, and Giersing in 7 of 23 [5]. Its nearest company is [[charcoal]], [[gunmetal]] and [[denim]] [5]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, and old varnish and soot darken dark pictures further, so a bluish black may be a black that aged [5].

openers: Before photography, naturalists matched a slug to Bluish Black, no. 18 in Werner's list.
Two historic systems disagree on what bluish black is: one dark purplish, one dark blue-green.

issues: Verified Werner no. 18 examples and Darwin hedge against Baty; no changes.
